questions.question: For $f(x,y) = 3x^2+4xy+5y^2$, which matrix is a symmetric associated matrix?

option_explanations: $\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$ fails to split $4xy$ into $2A_{12}$ (it uses $A_{12}=4$).

$\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$ drops the $4xy$ cross term.

questions.question: Why is the associated matrix of a quadratic form not unique?
options: Matrices with the same symmetric part give the same $\boldsymbol{x}^{\intercal}A\boldsymbol{x}$.
The matrix must always be diagonal.
The matrix must always be zero.
A quadratic form has no matrix expression whatsoever, in any form.
questions.explanation: Only the symmetric part of $A$ contributes to $x^\intercal A x$ (the antisymmetric part cancels), so any two matrices sharing the same symmetric part yield the same quadratic form, making the representation non-unique.
questions.source_support: The unique symmetric associated matrix is $(A+A^{\intercal})/2$.
option_explanations: The matrix need not be diagonal; e.g. $xy$ has symmetric associated matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac12\\\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix}$. Non-uniqueness arises because matrices with the same symmetric part give the same $\boldsymbol{x}^\intercal A\boldsymbol{x}$.

The matrix is not always zero; e.g. $x^2$ has associated matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0$. Non-uniqueness means different matrices can yield the same form, not that the matrix is zero.
A quadratic form has a matrix expression.
